opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we should be humble about how much harder humanoids are than something like ALOHA, and structure the research around that.

ALOHA was so successful partly because it was constrained. You have two arms, a fixed base, a tabletop, and a very intuitive teleoperation setup where the human's motion maps almost one-to-one onto the robot. That makes data collection cheap and high quality, and it lets you learn surprisingly dexterous behaviors with relatively simple imitation learning recipes. Once you move to a full humanoid, you're adding legs, balance, a torso, often many more degrees of freedom in the hands, and you're operating in an unstructured space instead of on a table. The action space explodes, the teleoperation problem gets much harder, and the cost of a failure goes up because the robot can actually fall over and break.

So a few principles I'd suggest. First, decompose where you can. You don't need a single end-to-end policy controlling every joint from pixels on day one. It's very reasonable to have a robust low-level controller for locomotion and balance, often trained in simulation with reinforcement learning, and then learn manipulation and higher-level behavior on top of that. Over time you can blur those boundaries, but starting with a stable foundation saves a lot of pain.

Second, take data seriously as the core bottleneck. With humanoids, the question of how you collect demonstrations at scale is really the central research problem. That means investing in better teleoperation interfaces, exoskeletons or VR-based systems, and also thinking hard about how to leverage human video, since humans and humanoids share a rough embodiment. That shared morphology is one of the strongest arguments for humanoids in the first place, so we should exploit it.

Third, lean on cross-embodiment and pretrained models. We've seen that training on data from many different robots helps, and vision-language models bring a lot of semantic understanding for free. A humanoid policy shouldn't have to learn what a cup is from scratch; it should inherit that and focus its limited robot data on the physical skills.

And finally, I'd encourage people to be clear-eyed about evaluation. Humanoid demos can look incredibly impressive in a video while being quite brittle in practice. Measuring reliability over many trials, in varied environments, is what will tell us whether we're actually making progress, rather than just producing compelling clips.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that ALOHA was kind of a gift in that it made the problem tractable. Two arms, a fixed base or a simple mobile base, a bimanual workspace that's roughly table-sized, and a teleop interface that's cheap and intuitive enough that you can collect tens of thousands of episodes without a huge ops team. A lot of the progress we've seen in imitation learning over the last couple of years is downstream of that simplification. You get to focus on the policy, the data, the architecture, and you don't have to think too hard about the embodiment.

Humanoids blow that up on several axes at once, and I think the mistake people make is treating it as "ALOHA plus legs." It's not additive, it's multiplicative. You have whole-body control, so now the policy has to reason about balance and contact with the floor while it's doing manipulation. You have way more degrees of freedom, which means your action space is bigger and your demonstrations are noisier. Teleop gets much harder, because mapping a human operator onto a body with different proportions and different joint limits is a real retargeting problem, and the data you get out is often not what a good policy would do. And the hardware is less mature, so the robot is changing under you while you're trying to learn on it.

So how should researchers approach that? A few things I'd say.

One, be very deliberate about decomposing the problem, at least initially. There's a strong temptation to say "end-to-end everything, let the model figure it out," and I'm sympathetic to that long-term, but right now I think it's reasonable to have a lower-level controller handle balance and locomotion, maybe trained with RL in sim, and have the learned manipulation policy operate on top of that abstraction. You can always collapse those layers later once you have enough data and the pieces are stable. Collapsing them too early means your manipulation data is contaminated with balance corrections, and you don't learn either thing well.

Two, think about data as the bottleneck, not the architecture. This is true across all of robot learning but it's acutely true for humanoids because collecting good whole-body data is so expensive. So you should be asking: what fraction of what I need can come from human video, from simulation, from other robot embodiments? The cross-embodiment transfer results we've seen suggest that a lot of the semantic and visual understanding transfers even when the kinematics don't. So I'd lean into pretraining on everything you can get and reserve the expensive humanoid teleop data for the last mile, the fine-tuning on the specific body.

Three, invest in evaluation early. With ALOHA you could kind of eyeball success on a handful of tasks. With a humanoid, the failure modes are more diverse, more dangerous, and harder to attribute. Did it fail because of the grasp, the balance controller, the retargeting, the vision? If you don't have infrastructure to answer that, you'll spend months chasing ghosts.

And then the last thing, which is maybe more philosophical: I'd push back a little on the framing that the complexity is purely added. Some of it is actually structure you can exploit. A humanoid body means your pretraining data from human videos matches your embodiment much more closely than it does for a two-armed robot bolted to a table. The kinematic prior is useful. So the question isn't just "how do we survive the added complexity," it's "where does the humanoid form factor give us leverage that we didn't have before," and designing the research program around that.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the complexity of the robot from the complexity of the learning problem. With a platform like ALOHA, you can focus on manipulation in a fairly controlled setting. With a humanoid, you’re also dealing with balance, locomotion, and how the whole body interacts with the environment. Those things are coupled: reaching for an object can change your balance, and where you stand changes what you can manipulate.

So I would approach it incrementally. Can we first get reliable manipulation with the humanoid standing in place? Then can we add movement and start studying tasks where moving actually matters? That gives you a way to understand which failures come from perception, which come from the learned policy, and which come from control.

And I wouldn’t assume that everything needs to be learned together from day one. You can use a reliable controller for balance while learning higher-level behaviors, and then explore tighter integration as the data and methods improve. The important thing is to build a setup where you can collect useful experience and measure progress. Otherwise, you add all this complexity, but it becomes very hard to tell what you’re learning from it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to be very deliberate about which complexity you introduce and what it buys you. With a platform like ALOHA, you can study a lot of manipulation while keeping the rest of the system relatively constrained. With a humanoid, suddenly you have to think about balance, locomotion, whole-body control, and how all of those interact with the manipulation task.

I would approach that incrementally. Can you get reliable manipulation first, then introduce mobility, and then study tasks that actually require coordinated whole-body behavior? Otherwise, if something fails, it’s very difficult to understand whether the problem is the learning algorithm, the data, the controller, or the hardware.

There’s also a question of what you ask the learned policy to handle. You don’t necessarily need to learn every aspect of control from scratch. You can build on reliable control systems and gradually expand what the policy is responsible for as you get better data and stronger evidence that it works.

So I’m excited about humanoids, but I think the research should be driven by capabilities and measurable progress. What tasks become possible because you have that embodiment, and can you learn them reliably across different environments? That’s the important test.
